title: Words Formed from Other Words
statement:
You are given a list of lowercase words. Some of the words can be built by gluing together **other words from the same list**; a word from the list may be used any number of times in one construction.

For every distinct word `w` in the list, find **all** the ways to split `w` into **two or more** consecutive pieces such that every piece is itself a word from the list. A split is the sequence of pieces from left to right, so `sun` + `rise` and `su` + `n` + `rise` are two different splits of `sunrise`. The trivial split consisting of the word alone does not count. Words that have no valid split are not reported.

Duplicates in the input list are ignored (each distinct word is considered once).

Report the result in this canonical order:

- words in increasing alphabetical (lexicographic) order;
- for the same word, its splits ordered by comparing the pieces from left to right as strings (so `[su, n, rise]` comes before `[sun, rise]`, because `su` is smaller than `sun`).

**Follow-up:** the original question asks for a map from each such word to the list of its splits. The output format below is a flat, sorted version of that map.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The next tokens contain `n` words separated by whitespace (they may be spread over several lines).
outputFormat:
First print `T`, the total number of lines that follow (the total number of valid splits over all words).
Then print `T` lines, one per split, in the canonical order described above. Each line has the form `word: piece1 piece2 ... piecek` (the word, a colon, a space, then the pieces separated by single spaces). If no word has a valid split, print `0` only.
constraints: 1 ≤ length of each word ≤ 30; words consist of lowercase letters `a`-`z`
The total number of valid splits over all words is at most 30000

examples.input:
7
cat cats dog catsdog s dogcat catdog
examples.output:
5
catdog: cat dog
cats: cat s
catsdog: cat s dog
catsdog: cats dog
dogcat: dog cat
examples.explanation: `catsdog` splits as `cat` + `s` + `dog` and as `cats` + `dog`; the first is listed first since `cat` < `cats`. `catdog`, `cats` and `dogcat` have one split each. `cat`, `dog` and `s` cannot be built from other words.

examples.input:
14
happy rise for set sunrise sun su nset sunset mind happymind n rise happysunrise
examples.output:
11
happymind: happy mind
happysunrise: happy su n rise
happysunrise: happy sun rise
happysunrise: happy sunrise
nset: n set
sun: su n
sunrise: su n rise
sunrise: sun rise
sunset: su n set
sunset: su nset
sunset: sun set
examples.explanation: `rise` appears twice but counts once. `sunrise` can be built as `su n rise` or `sun rise`, and `sunset` in three ways: `su n set`, `su nset` and `sun set`. `happysunrise` has three splits (`happy su n rise`, `happy sun rise`, `happy sunrise`), `happymind` is `happy mind`, `nset` is `n set` and `sun` is `su n`. `happy`, `rise`, `for`, `set`, `su`, `n` and `mind` cannot be built from other words.
No word is made from other words in the list, so only `0` is printed.

hints: Put all words in a hash set. For one word at a time, you need to enumerate every way to cut it into pieces that are all in the set.
Plain backtracking can waste time exploring prefixes that can never be completed. First compute, from right to left, which suffix positions can be split into valid pieces (a word-break DP).

Then backtrack from position 0, only taking cuts that lead to a position from which the rest can be finished. Remember to skip the cut that takes the whole word as a single piece, and try shorter pieces first to get the required order for free.
